items.originalTitle: Why the World’s Climate Talks Broke Down—and What Happens Now
items.author: T. Michelle Murphy
items.title: Why the World’s Climate Talks Broke Down—and What Happens Now
items.summary: COP31 President Murat Kurum speaks during a plenary session at the COP31 UN Climate Summit on Nov. 11, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. —Khalil Hamra—AP COP31 , the United Nations’ annual climate change summit, ended on Sunday without consensus on an overarching climate deal after about two days of overtime in Antalya, Türkiye. The annual conference brings together delegates to shape and formalize an approach to combating the effects of global warming . This year, the main dispute was whether the agreement should explicitly call for a transition away from fossil fuels . That commitment traces back to the Paris Agreement , a 2015 climate treaty that calls for efforts to limit global warming to 1.5°C (2.7°F) above preindustrial levels. Read more: Climate Change Is Accelerating Faster Than We Can Respond, Scientists Warn Among the countries that opposed language calling for a transition away from fossil fuels were Russia and Saudi Arabia, while the European Union, the United Kingdom, and others refused to agree to any deals that did not acknowledge the leading cause of climate change. COP31’s President Murat Kurum announced on Sunday that a deal had not been reached. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognize that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted,” he said . Australia’s Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen was a co-leader at the event, acting as President of Negotiations. “Unfortunately we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision and that’s very disappointing,” he said Sunday. Failure to reach an agreement is not unheard of, but it is uncommon; the last comparable deadlock was in Copenhagen in 2009. At the time, an irreconcilable clash emerged over which countries should cut greenhouse gas emissions, how deep those cuts should be, and whether the commitments should be legally binding. “Despite the range of expectations among states going into COP31, no delegation left believing it had been a win,” says Lavanya Rajamani, a professor of international environmental law at the University of Oxford who helped draft the Paris Agreement. For Rajamani, the impasse shows how far apart the science and the politics of climate action have become. “While such divergences are not new to the process, the gap has never been wider,” she says. The world is on track to imminently exceed 1.5°C of warming, Rajamani adds, just as governments are showing a “rapidly dwindling appetite” for difficult and potentially costly action. That puts growing strain on a summit built around consensus. What is COP31? The Conference of the Parties (COP) is the annual meeting of countries that are party to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The U.N. climate summit originated in Berlin in 1995. The host location typically rotates, with recent summits taking place in Dubai, United Arab Emirates (2023); Baku, Azerbaijan (2024); and Belém, Brazil (2025). COP31 was scheduled for Nov. 9 through Nov. 20 in Antalya, but reached a record-setting overtime that kept the summit in progress through Nov. 22. Most countries sent delegations to COP31. Israel’s environment ministry said its officials would participate remotely, citing security concerns about sending a delegation to Antalya. The United States did not send an official delegation for the second year in a row. In January, it withdrew from the Paris Agreement. As COP31 was preparing to open in early November, a White House official told Spectrum News that the summit “rejects reality” and said the Trump Administration was pursuing an “energy dominance agenda.” In Antalya, the countries at the table faced a different question: how to turn years of climate pledges into action. “Over the past few years, international climate negotiations have shifted from a focus on establishing rules and making promises to ensuring implementation and delivery. This phase was always going to be challenging—it is where the rubber hits the road,” Rajamani says. Broad language can smooth over disagreements, she continues, but it gets harder to find common ground when countries have to decide what to do and who will pay for it. Why did the COP31 climate talks break down? One of the biggest disputes at COP31 was whether the agreement should explicitly call for a shift away from fossil fuels. A draft released early Sunday would have been the first U.N. climate summit agreement to acknowledge that global warming is on track to exceed 1.5°C above preindustrial levels in the coming years. It also welcomed faster development of technologies that remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, with the aim of eventually bringing warming back below that threshold. The draft referred back to the 2023 Dubai agreement as a whole, without explicitly restating its call to transition away from fossil fuels. “It’s unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,” Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said on behalf of the EU on Sunday. Burning coal, oil, and gas is the main cause of global warming, according to the United Nations , accounting for around 68% of global greenhouse gas emissions and nearly 90% of all carbon dioxide emissions. That warming is making heat waves more intense and causing sea levels to rise. “The question is not so much what an explicit mention would have accomplished, but what its absence would have implied,” Rajamani explains. “The 2023 UAE consensus recognized the need to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems—yet subsequent COP decisions have failed to advance, or even reaffirm, this commitment.” Meanwhile, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said in its 2025 advisory opinion on climate change that failure to take appropriate action on fossil fuel production, consumption, exploration licences, and subsidies may constitute an internationally wrongful act, she points out. “The 2026 Santa Marta Initiative on transitioning away from fossil fuels is also gaining momentum,” she adds, referring to an April 2026 conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, where 57 countries gathered to discuss how to move away from fossil fuels. “Against this backdrop, omitting fossil fuels from a COP cover decision would signal a retreat from the transition,” Rajamani says. “Explicit language, provided it did not weaken the UAE Consensus, would instead have reinforced growing momentum and sent an important signal to markets and policymakers.” Climate finance was another sticking point. The Least Developed Countries group said the draft fell short on funding to help vulnerable countries adapt to climate change. The African Group of Negotiators, which represents 54 African countries, questioned whether the proposed roadmap would deliver that funding. The group was still willing to accept the draft as a compromise. Delegates rejected a separate draft decision on the Mitigation Work Programme, which gives countries a forum to discuss how to cut greenhouse gas emissions faster and where investment is needed. At COP31, countries disagreed over how long to extend the program and how closely to tie it to the U.N.’s global assessment of climate progress. Delegates ultimately rejected the draft decision. Delegates did, however, reach agreement on a “just transition” decision, which focuses on how to make the move to a low-carbon economy fair to workers and communities affected by the shift. The dispute at COP31 was over what a U.N. mechanism to support that work should do, how it should operate, and how it would be funded. The decision leaves operational details to be worked out in 2027. They also adopted separate decisions on the Adaptation Fund and the Global Goal on Adaptation. Rajamani says the overarching deal fell apart in part because some countries were more willing than in the past to reject an agreement they saw as too weak. They worry that downplaying climate damage, while prioritizing technological fixes over urgent emissions cuts and support, could undermine climate action in the long run. What happens next? Rajamani observes a “growing frustration with the time-intensive, consensus-based negotiating process,” and she says that it yields weak outcomes that are “radically out of step with the science and the scale and severity of climate impacts already unfolding.” Youth advocates voiced their own frustration at the summit’s closing session. Oumnia Anfer, a youth representative at COP31, took the floor to address negotiators. “You have let us down,” she said . “We refuse to bear the consequences of your lack of ambition.” “Some states, including those most vulnerable to climate change, appear to have reached the limits of their patience with the process,” Rajamani explains. She points out that a failure to reach an agreement simply punts decisions further down the road, saying: “All these issues will return to the agenda at the next COP.” COP32 is scheduled to take place in November 2027 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. “Parties will return for the next round of the boxing match in Addis Ababa next year,” Rajamani says. “In the meantime, growing frustration and exasperation with the multilateral negotiating process are likely to drive greater attention towards climate litigation—which has yielded far more progressive and climate-friendly outcomes, including at the highest judicial level, the ICJ—and climate action beyond the state.” Ireland and Tuvalu plan to co-host a follow-up to the Santa Marta conference on moving away from fossil fuels before COP32. Both meetings are months away. At Sunday’s closing session in Antalya, Kurum pointed to the urgency of the work still ahead. “Climate change does not follow our negotiating schedule,” he said, before gaveling the summit to an end.

items.summary: Adults with heart disease who sleep nine or more hours per night could be at a higher risk of death from both heart-related and non-heart-related causes than those who sleep seven to eight hours, according to a recent study. The cohort study in the journal PLOS One, titled "Sleep duration and cause-specific mortality among US adults with heart disease," analyzed data from 3,287 adults with heart disease from the 2004 National Health Survey linked to the National Death Index running until Dec. 31, 2019. In the National Health Survey, participants answered whether they had heart disease based on if they had ever been told they had coronary heart disease, a heart attack or a heart condition or disease, according to the study. MORE NAPS, HIGHER RISK? RESEARCH LINKS DAYTIME SLEEP TO HEALTH WARNINGS IN AGING ADULTS "Sleep affects blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, inflammation, and appetite hormones, and all of these influence cardiovascular risk," Erin Palinksi-Wade, a New Jersey-based registered dietitian and Certified Diabetes Care and Education Specialist (CDCES), told Fox News Digital. The study authors adjusted for health factors and lifestyle behaviors such as body mass index (BMI), alcohol consumption, smoking, physical activity, diabetes, hypertension and more. Sleep per 24 hours was categorized into durations of six hours or less, seven to eight hours and nine or more hours. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Over approximately 15 years of follow-up, 49.4% of participants died. Out of all participants, 16.7% died from heart-related causes and 32.6% died from non-heart-related causes. After adjusting for all lifestyle factors, researchers found that sleeping nine or more hours was linked to a higher mortality risk, compared with sleeping seven to eight hours. There was a 51% increased risk of all causes of death, a 53% increased risk of heart-related causes of death and a 50% increased risk of non-heart-related mortality. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Sleep duration of six hours or less was significantly associated with non-heart-related death only in the least-adjusted model, and the connection weakened with further adjustment. "Because the study is observational, it shows an association, not cause and effect. Long sleep may be a symptom of underlying problems like more advanced heart disease, depression, sleep apnea , or medication side effects, and the study couldn't fully account for those," Palinski-Wade said. The authors noted that their findings do not invalidate the negative cardiovascular effects of getting too little sleep. "I'm not aware of a convincing biological mechanism by which extra hours of sleep damage the heart," Antony Chu, MD, a cardiologist and clinical assistant professor at Brown University’s Warren Alpert School of Medicine, told Fox News Digital. "What I see clinically is that patients sleep longer because something is pulling on their reserve: worsening heart failure, untreated obstructive or central sleep apnea, depression, sedating medications, anemia or frailty," Chu said. Sleeping too much or too little are both potential red flags, Palinski-Wade noted, so it’s important for people to pay attention to how rested they feel rather than only focusing on the number of hours they slept. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Because the study only tested people with pre-existing heart conditions, it should not be used to suggest that prolonged sleep leads to heart disease in the general population, she added.

items.originalTitle: How to Deal with Anxiety
items.author: Joan M. Cook
items.title: How to Deal with Anxiety
items.summary: —Creative Images Lab—Getty Images Hands down, anxiety is the most common mental health issue affecting Americans today. Over 19% of adults in the U.S. meet criteria for an anxiety disorder in any given year. Many often don’t recognize these difficulties, or mistake them for signs of a physical health condition. As a psychologist, I can tell you that worrying is a normal part of life. Occasionally, we all get a little nervous about something. We can fret that we blew a job interview or made a poor impression on a first date. We may feel on edge thinking about a big purchase we need to make and concerned about how we are going to pay for it. Many of us have concerns about money and finances, including how we are going to pay off a mortgage or a big debt. We may experience uneasiness about our relationships, including conflict with a partner or tension with an aging parent. We may be nervous about upcoming deadlines at work or national elections. Other times, our anxiety may be more free-floating, overly intense concerns latching on to any number of things. It’s hard to know how to safely stop the worry cycle, so we often, as humans, over-prepare, try to control a situation, or avoid it altogether. But when anxiety persists and gets worse over time, when it impairs our ability to function on the job or in the classroom, or our ability to connect with others, anxiety becomes problematic and potentially diagnosable. “Anxiety makes people’s lives smaller as they prune all the bits of their lives that lead to anxiety,” says Debra Kaysen , a psychologist and professor at Stanford University. “That works short-term, but long-term steals all the parts of life that give joy.” The great news is that there are effective treatments. Several free, reliable screens can help people do a self-assessment regarding whether they may meet criteria for an anxiety disorder. Though there are a range of anxiety disorders —including generalized anxiety, panic, phobias, and obsessive-compulsive disorder—most have similar underlying causes. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) can help to identify and manage the factors that contribute to anxiety. By learning to change unhelpful thought patterns, we can reduce the frequency and intensity of anxious symptoms. We can also learn techniques to regulate our anxiety and help us engage in effective problem-solving. That said, it isn’t always easy to get the help we need. There are a host of barriers, from financial, transportation, and scheduling to stigma, poor access, and limited availability. Anne Marie Albano , a psychologist and professor at Columbia University, has spent decades conducting research on and treating anxiety in children, adolescents, and young adults. Along with her colleagues, Albano developed several effective interventions, including Coaching Approach Behavior and Leading by Modeling (CALM) for families with young children to help them master circumstances that trigger intense discomfort, as well as the Launching Emerging Adults Program (LEAP), which centers on assisting individuals as they work through anxiety during the transition to adulthood. Albano recommends practicing breathing techniques to manage anxiety. “Close your eyes and focus on a quiet or pleasant scene in your mind. Breathe in slowly while counting to three, then pause a second, and then breathe out to the count of three. Breathing slowly and deeply, do this for ten repetitions,” she says. The benefit of this technique is that it’s endlessly versatile. “It’s a quick strategy that once learned, you can use with your eyes open and in any situation. Parents can even do this with their children to teach them belly breathing,” Albano explains. “Adults can use this before meetings or other emotionally challenging situations to regulate themselves and manage not just anxiety but other strong emotions.” In addition to breathing exercises, physical activity is one of the best ways to lessen anxiety for people of all ages. “Getting outside each day, rain or shine, and being physically active and social will build your natural resilience and coping skills. Walking, shooting hoops, yoga, swimming, and especially doing these things with other people will strengthen your physical capacity to manage stress and provide you with social networking and support from others,” Albano lists. Even just 10 or 15 minutes a day can help us feel more calm and capable. Even if, for whatever reason, someone is unable to access formal mental health services, there are things we can do to help ourselves with intense apprehension or looming thoughts of threat, trouble, or catastrophe. In my view, an excellent resource is the Association for Behavioral and Cognitive Therapies , an interdisciplinary organization of professionals dedicated to the study of behavioral health. The website has research-based information in English and Spanish about anxiety disorders , treatments , and a therapist directory . Anxiety is common and treatable. The National Institute of Mental Health also offers a wealth of information on anxiety , including free digital brochures and fact sheets , updates from the latest research, and how to find help and support . Help is out there, and if you have persistent anxiety, rest assured you are not alone.

items.originalTitle: Scoop: The Pentagon's case for Canada to "get serious" on defense
items.author: Marc Caputo
items.title: Scoop: The Pentagon's case for Canada to "get serious" on defense
items.summary: The Pentagon accused Canada of failing to become a "credible partner" due to its faltering military readiness and low defense spending, according to a sharply worded fact sheet issued by the Pentagon to justify new restrictions on America's northern neighbor. Why it matters: The restrictions deepen tensions between the U.S. and Canada over trade and defense, as Ottawa reconsiders billions of dollars in purchases of American weapons. The new restraints — which do not affect defense or intelligence sharing— limit U.S. military personnel from fraternizing with their Canadian counterparts at official events without prior authorization from the Pentagon, an official told Axios. The Pentagon fact sheet has not been reported. But the Washington Post first reported the restrictions, followed by the New York Times . Zoom in: At the heart of the dispute are NATO defense spending goals and military readiness under the bilateral North American Aerospace Defense Command where, the memo says, Canada falls short in three ways: 🛩️ Air: Only 41.9% of the Royal Canadian Air Force fleet "was serviceable from 2025-2026, largely due to ageing equipment and personnel shortages," the Pentagon fact sheet says. The shortfall limits Canada's "ability to meaningfully contribute to air defense commitments … to defend our North American airspace against all threats." Canada relies on the U.S. and NATO for airborne early-warning aircraft but is negotiating to buy its own from Sweden's Saab. ⚓️ Sea: Just 53.9% of Canada's naval fleet was "serviceable" from 2025-2026, limiting its "ability to monitor maritime approaches to North America," the fact sheet says. Only one of Canada's "four ageing Victoria-class submarines" is "seaworthy at any given time." Canada has a new fleet of conventional submarines, manufactured by ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems, coming on line, but until then, its undersea "capability will be limited." 🪖 Land: The Canadian Army had an operational readiness rate of 48% from 2025-2026. The other side: Canada's own defense department reported the same equipment shortages while finding that 61% of its military units were ready for operations. Canada's defense ministry could not be reached. Friction point : NATO defense spending has been a constant sore spot for President Trump. Canada first agreed to spend 2% of GDP on defense spending in 2006, but it was only at 1.5% until 2025, according to the Pentagon. Canada announced in March that it had achieved 2% GDP-defense spending, but now the target is 5% by 2035 and U.S. policy makers say Ottawa "has yet to articulate a resourced path to reach this target. "Canada must get serious and focused," the fact sheet said. The big picture: More defense spending by NATO allies is a revenue generator for the U.S., which has the globe's largest military-industrial complex. "Since March 2025," the Pentagon fact sheet noted, "Ottawa has been reviewing its decision to procure 88 F-35s to replace its ageing fighters and is considering a mixed fleet that will compound existing personnel shortfalls." Canada is increasingly looking to European manufacturers for its military buildup. Context: Relations between the two countries soured when Trump scrapped a free-trade agreement he insisted on in his first term, began a tariff war and threatened to annex Canada as the 51st state. At a Friday news conference, Trump complained about Canada and trade imbalances between the two countries. The bottom line: The two nations remain allies and work closely together on defense issues. Canada has an office in the Pentagon next to the joint staff. The limited restrictions imposed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on official interactions between U.S. and Canadian personnel are a "shot across the bow," a U.S. official said. "Unfortunately," the Pentagon fact sheet said, "Canada has yet to make the hard decisions and tradeoffs needed to put it on track to fulfill its NATO Defense Investment Pledge and become a credible partner in the defense of our shared continent. Canada's defense shortfalls speak for themselves."

items.originalTitle: High-end genealogy travel is booming, offering luxe journeys to the roots of your family tree
items.author: Adam Erace
items.title: High-end genealogy travel is booming, offering luxe journeys to the roots of your family tree
items.summary: My great-great-grandfather came to the Tuscan ghost island of Pianosa as a prisoner. I arrived there on a luxury vacation. The island lives up to its name, I thought as my ferry drifted toward the sole dock on this protected isola fantasma . “Pianosa” is derived from piano , Italian for “flat,” and indeed the island crouches low to the cyan Tyrrhenian Sea , its shores fringed by parasol pines and deserted prison watchtowers. From 1856 to 1998, Pianosa was a remote penal colony—and the place where my ancestor, Salvatore Giovanni Pellegrino Irace, died. I’d learned this family lore thanks to a partnership between Ancestry, the Blackstone-owned leader in the at-home DNA-testing space, and Kensington, a bespoke travel outfitter, which invited me to test-drive its Personal Heritage Journey. After I submitted a DNA sample, Ancestry got to work filling in my Italian family tree, with researchers combing archives in Tuscany, Molise, and Campania. “So the interesting thing about Salvatore,” genealogist Kyle Betit said on our initial call, “is that he died in prison of tuberculosis in 1894—and we don’t know why he was there.” Who doesn’t love a good family mystery? That’s part of what draws clients to Kensington’s genealogical-based trips. The journeys average $20,000 to $25,000 per person, with the company’s travel desk handling all the details in high style. San Gennaro, the main church in Praiano, on the Amalfi Coast. Adam Erace for Fortune For me, that meant a chartered boat from mainland Tuscany to the island of Elba; chauffeured SUVs between regions; a private guide in Pompeii; and some spectacular accommodations, including Casa Angelina and Palazzo Avino on the Amalfi Coast. The major flex, though, was having a professional genealogist, Gabriele Musumeci, riding shotgun. Once upon a time, possessing one’s comprehensive genealogy was a signal of wealth and pedigree. Then, in the 2000s, the rise of at-home DNA-testing kits from Ancestry and 23andMe made such knowledge commonplace. The ultrawealthy can now seek out deeper stories through first-person ancestry tourism, from China to Ghana. Kensington reports that demand has doubled and revenue has quadrupled in five years. Grand View Research put the global value of “heritage tourism”—of which ancestral travel is a segment—at $625 billion in 2025. It’s expected to reach almost a trillion by 2033. “I think there’s a deep need in any of us to understand who we are,” Musumeci said as we descended the concrete steps to Pianosa’s white-sand beach, Cala Giovanna. “For most Americans, your story is cut.” He made a chopping motion. And then a sewing motion: “We stitch it back together.” Pianosa Island. Adam Erace for Fortune Most luxury travel planners now offer some variety of ancestry service. Alexandrea Padilha, director at the membership-based Fischer Unlimited, recently hired genealogists in Germany and the U.S. to trace a Louisiana tech entrepreneur’s ancestry. The results were bound into a book for the client’s father’s 80th birthday and also informed the itinerary for a trip to Germany—a way to show younger family members their roots. “I think that’s grounding for young adults today,” Padilha says, “living in a world that’s slowly slipping away.” Existential dread is one hell of a motivator. “When it feels like the world may be shifting every second, people reach for something enduring,” says Dr. Katie Blake, a Texas-based social psychologist who specializes in travel. “The archives give you the facts, but it’s the place itself that gives you the identity pull that’s different than something you just see on paper.” A sudden, biblical rainstorm broke open during our mile-long bike ride from Cala Giovanna to Pianosa’s imposing Agrippa Prison. We sheltered inside the Zante wing, where prisoners like Salvatore slept four to a concrete cell on metal beds, as thunder rattled the rusty gates. My itinerary traced Salvatore’s life backward. A few days later, Musumeci and I rendezvoused in Molise, where Salvatore grew up. My great-great-great-grandfather, Vincenzo, moved his family to Montenero di Bisaccia, a mountain keep surrounded by vineyards and wheat fields sloping down to the Adriatic, in 1838, when Salvatore was a boy. At Montenero’s city hall, the clerks hauled out massive, crimson-bound books, and Musumeci leafed through until he found the birth and marriage records of Salvatore’s second son, Giuseppe—my great-grandfather. An alley in Montenero. Adam Erace for Fortune Walking through Montenero’s hilltop puzzle of alleys brought those pieces of paper to life—and conjured a story of downward mobility. Along the town’s outer promenade, ringing the remains of medieval stone walls, a lookout faced the amber foothills where Vincenzo bought land and a farmhouse. I walked the narrow alley the family lived on after they lost the farm. Within four years, Vincenzo had spiraled from merchant and farm owner to street sweeper. He died in 1842, leaving his son on the poverty-to-prison pipeline. I also saw the house in the old ghetto where my great-grandmother, Nicoletta, grew up. She and Giuseppe had a daughter out of wedlock, Mattia. (Nobody in my family had known Mattia existed until Musumeci discovered her.) The infant likely died during the couple’s 1900 journey to America, where, at Ellis Island, Irace became Erace. Giuseppe and Nicoletta settled in Philadelphia and had 16—yes, 16—more children, including my paternal grandfather, Michael Erace, who died in 2013. It was like I was looking at Grandpop Mike’s long-lost brother when we met Bruno Irace, a 74-year-old Ironman triathlete and my fourth cousin, that afternoon. Smile, hair, complexion, bone structure; it was uncanny. We sipped espresso and compared photos, then visited a cemetery where “Irace” seemed to be engraved on every other gravestone. Two Iraces were listed on an obelisk in the village park honoring fallen soldiers. When it was time to leave Montenero, Bruno told us to come back soon. “You have family here,” he said. The name Irace was also everywhere in the archives of San Luca, the family’s neighborhood church, in Praiano, on the Amalfi Coast, the final stop on my journey. This dramatic shoreline of improbable cliff-top villages and citrus groves set high above the sapphire sea is one of the most beautiful places in the world. I couldn’t help but wonder about the Iraces: Why did these fools leave? What misfortune befell my reasonably prosperous ancestors to make them abscond from this stunning seaside real estate? Musumeci had coordinated with the pastor, who granted us free rein of his office, a charmingly cluttered room with sea views through diamond-paned windows. Hundreds of books, some dating to the 1600s, filled a tall cabinet, their yellowed pages brittle as autumn leaves. Handwritten in meticulous script were the births and baptisms, marriages and deaths of San Luca’s parishioners, which included generations of Iraces. Genealogist Musumeci reading records. Adam Erace for Fortune “Oh, wow … ” Musumeci stopped suddenly as his finger moved across a page. He pointed to Vincenzo’s marriage record. “Adam, the date … ” October 10, 1807. It took a few seconds to dawn on me. I checked my phone: October 10, 2026. Exactly 219 years earlier, Vincenzo Irace and Mariangela Rispoli, ages 21 and 18, had stood at San Luca’s resplendent altar and exchanged vows. Until then, I’d encountered Vincenzo mostly through his losses: his farm, his livelihood, his family’s good name. Here was a record of a beginning. Whatever came later, my great-great-great-grandparents had first been two young people at the altar of a church above the sea. I hadn’t found all the answers in Italy. We never learned why they left the Amalfi Coast, what sent their son to prison, or what compelled their grandson to cross an ocean. The private guides, chauffeured SUVs, and beautiful hotels couldn’t make the records yield answers they didn’t contain. But the distance between my ancestors’ lives and my own no longer seemed quite so great. Standing in San Luca, I wasn’t the discerning traveler whose preferences shaped the itinerary. For all the choices I’d made on this trip, the ones that mattered most had been made two centuries earlier. For once, the point wasn’t being made to feel important. The real privilege was the opportunity to feel very, very small. This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027 issue of Fortune with the headline “The most exclusive itinerary is written in your DNA.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.title: Massive 17-foot shark comes face-to-face with scientists in incredible deep-sea footage
items.summary: A video making the rounds on social media Sunday shows a massive deep-water shark getting up close and personal with a group of scientists inside a submersible. And when I say up close and personal , I mean it. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS In the footage, the shark slowly circles the vessel, seemingly just as curious about its human visitors as they are about her. At one point, she swims right up to the viewing window and presses her snout against the glass. The video is spectacular, but it isn't new. The encounter actually happened back in June 2019, roughly 1,700 feet beneath the surface of the Atlantic Ocean near the Bahamas. Check out the piercing blue eye at the 52-second mark. The shark is a bluntnose sixgill, a deep-water species that can grow up to 20 feet long. Researchers estimated that the particularly inquisitive female in the video measured about 16-17 feet. And as incredible as the footage is, the story behind it might be even cooler. The encounter occurred during an expedition by OceanX, an ocean exploration organization working alongside marine scientists to study the bluntnose sixgill shark . The team traveled to the deep waters of Exuma Sound aboard the research vessel Alucia, hoping to accomplish something that had never been done before: attach a satellite tracking tag to a sixgill shark without bringing it to the surface. THE BIGGEST NAMES AND WILDEST STORIES IN THE GREAT OUTDOORS. WATCH 'OPEN SEASON' ON YOUTUBE! Previously, researchers studying these animals had to capture them and haul them up from the depths. But that process can stress the sharks and disrupt their natural behavior, making it difficult to collect reliable data about how they actually live. Using OceanX's three-person submersible, Nadir, the team descended into the darkness with roughly 100 pounds of bait to attract the sharks. After several unsuccessful attempts involving bad weather, equipment problems and even a grouper that interfered with the tagging process, the researchers finally got their chance on June 29. According to the Florida Museum of Natural History , scientist Gavin Naylor successfully attached a satellite tag to a male sixgill shark more than 1,700 feet underwater. It was the first time scientists had successfully tagged one at depth in its natural habitat. But the team also encountered several other sharks during the dive, including the enormous female that stars in the viral video. FORREST GALANTE SAYS MOST SHARK BITES ARE A CASE OF MISTAKEN IDENTITY AS FLORIDA ATTACKS LEAD THE US "She was studying us," Naylor told the Florida Museum. "It was delightful for me to see a shark being curious. We'd be arrogant to think we were the only ones doing the evaluating." Bluntnose sixgill sharks are among the largest predatory sharks in the ocean, although most people will never see one. That's because these animals spend much of their lives hundreds or even thousands of feet below the surface. Some have been documented at depths approaching 6,500 feet. They're also pretty much living fossils . According to the Florida Museum, sixgills closely resemble sharks that swam the oceans roughly 200 million years ago. Way down there, sixgills aren't generally a threat to humans. They spend their days hunting fish, squid and other marine life, occasionally scavenging larger carcasses. items.summary: "48 Hours" correspondents Anne-Marie Green and Peter Van Sant discuss the murder of Susan Lane, known as Phoenix, near Oregon's Mount Hood. They explore the community's tradition of "mountain justice," the local search efforts that led to the discovery of Phoenix's body, and the investigation into her husband, Michel Fournier, whose changing stories and suspicious alibis helped unravel the case.

items.title: Jim Beam to pause production at flagship Kentucky distillery in major shift for iconic American whiskey brand
items.summary: Jim Beam will indefinitely pause production at its historic flagship distillery in Clermont, Kentucky, amid declining whiskey sales and record inventories. The iconic American whiskey brand, owned by Japanese multinational brewing and distilling company Suntory Global Spirits , announced last December that it would pause production at its Clermont, Kentucky facility for one year, with plans to resume operations in 2027, Food Dive reported. However, in a new development, it is now uncertain when the Clermont distillery will begin operations again, the company told The Courier Journal. NEW 123.4-PROOF WHISKEY PROMPTS EXPERT WARNING THAT STRONGER ISN'T ALWAYS BETTER Suntory told the outlet that it manages its Kentucky production in accordance with demand, inventory and long-term needs. The company noted that it plans to reassess production needs in the future. In the meantime, Jim Beam has moved production to its nearby Booker Noe Distillery in Boston, Kentucky, which, with an output of 45 million original proof gallons annually, is the brand’s largest distillery, according to Food Dive. Noe distillery, located on the Clermont facility's campus, will continue its operations producing whiskey labels including Knob Creek, Little Book and Booker's, Inc. reported. Fox News Digital reached out to Jim Beam and the brand’s parent company, Suntory Holdings, for comment. Jim Beam’s move comes amid an ongoing decrease in consumer demand for whiskey , with large quantities of the spirit sitting untouched. Whiskey inventory in the U.S. is three times higher than estimated annual demand, global beverage alcohol data and insight firm IWSR reported in October. "And in most cases, that growth is concentrating at the premium end, while the mainstream and value tiers absorb the pain," he added. items.originalTitle: FBI investigates apparent hack of critical crime database
items.title: FBI investigates apparent hack of critical crime database
items.summary: The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center, two people briefed on the matter told NBC News. The FBI’s National Crime Information Center is used to connect federal, state and local authorities so that important law enforcement information is available nationwide. NBC News’ Julie Tsirkin reports.
